title: The Penalty Students Pay for Using AI
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Benjamin Riley contrasts generative AI with earlier ed-tech, which suffered from what Laurence Holt called the 5 Percent Problem of too few students using programs as intended. Students have embraced AI widely, so dosage is not the issue, yet rigorous research on its effects has been scarce. Riley examines a new working paper by David Strömberg, Victor Lei, and Yanhui Wu that tracked about 27,000 Chinese secondary students as roughly 80 percent adopted generative AI. Within five months about half fully outsourced their homework, spending less time and earning higher homework scores while performance fell sharply on closed-book tests and on high school and college entrance exams. Finding no corresponding learning benefit, Riley names this the 50 Percent Problem and warns that AI creates a mental masquerade in which scores rise while actual learning declines.
points: A Stanford landscape review found only about 20 of more than 800 studies of AI in education produced credible causal evidence.
The Chinese study captured AI adoption dates by having students record registration dates for AI tools on their devices.
About half of AI-using students engaged in full homework outsourcing after five months of use.
By June 2025 performance fell 24 percent on the high school entrance exam and 18 percent on the college entrance exam.
Riley warns that when classmates boost grades with AI, even reluctant students feel pressured into a cognitive race to the bottom.
quotes: Generative AI does not suffer from this problem. Uniquely perhaps in the history of ed-tech, AI has been broadly embraced by students worldwide, to the point the phrase “AI is inevitable” has become commonplace in education discourse.

There are notable exceptions— such as these —but a recent research landscape analysis out of Stanford indicated that, out of more than 800 studies of AI in education, a mere 20 produced credible causal evidence.

After just five months of use, approximately 50 percent of these students engaged in “full homework outsourcing,” meaning, they essentially stopped doing their homework independently and used AI instead.
By the end of June 2025, overall student performance fell by 24 percent on the high school entrance exam and 18 percent on the college entrance exam—a massive decline.

In homage to Laurence Holt’s 5 Percent Problem, I have taken to calling this finding the “50 Percent Problem,” a conservative measure of the harm stemming from widespread AI adoption by students, rather than their failure to use it.
In this sense, AI fosters a mental masquerade as scores go up while actual learning goes down.
